summary: A struct groups values of different types under one name, giving each member its own storage; a union overlays its members in the same bytes so only one is meaningful at a time; an enum names a set of integer constants. Together they model records, variants and states, and they are the building blocks of linked lists, trees, protocol headers, device registers and interpreters. Knowing how they are laid out, copied, initialized and combined (tagged unions) is core C interview material.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Arrays hold many values of one type. Real data is heterogeneous: a student has a name, an age and a grade; a network packet has fields of several widths; a token is either a number or a string. C answers with three user-defined types. A **struct** puts members side by side. A **union** puts them on top of each other. An **enum** gives readable names to small integers. They are declared with a tag (`struct Student`) and usually shortened with `typedef`.
bullets: **Struct**: all members exist at once; size is at least the sum of the member sizes.
**Union**: one member active at a time; size equals the largest member (plus padding).
**Enum**: a type whose values are named integer constants; the compiler just substitutes numbers.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
bullets: **Member**: a named field inside a struct or union. Members may be scalars, arrays, pointers or other aggregates.
**Tag**: the name after `struct`, `union` or `enum`. `struct Point` is the full type name; the tag lives in a separate namespace from variables.
**Dot operator `.`**: selects a member of a struct value. **Arrow operator `->`**: selects a member through a pointer; `p->x` means `(*p).x`.
**Initializer list**: `{a, b, c}` assigns members in declaration order. **Designated initializer** (C99): `{.age = 18, .name = "Anu"}` in any order; omitted members become zero.
**Default state**: an automatic struct with no initializer holds garbage; one with any initializer has every unmentioned member zeroed; static structs are zeroed.
**Struct assignment**: `b = a;` copies every member byte for byte (a shallow copy: pointers are copied, not their targets).
**Padding**: unused bytes inserted so each member sits at an address that suits its alignment, so `sizeof(struct)` can exceed the sum of members.
**Self-referential struct**: contains a pointer to its own type, the foundation of lists and trees.
**Union**: members share one address; writing one overwrites the others.
**Tagged union**: a struct holding an enum that says which union member is valid.
**Enumeration constant**: an identifier such as `RUNNING` with type `int` and a fixed value; it is a compile-time constant usable in `case` labels and array sizes.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.body: A struct variable occupies one contiguous block. Each member sits at a fixed offset from the start, in declaration order, so the compiler turns `s.age` into 'base address plus offset'. The program below shows initialization, pointer access, copying and passing by value versus by pointer.
bullets: **Layout example**: `struct { char c; int n; }` places `c` at offset 0, three padding bytes, then `n` at offset 4, so `sizeof` is 8, not 5.
**Union write and read**: after `union U { int i; float f; } u; u.f = 1.0f;` reading `u.i` returns `0x3f800000` (1065353216), the IEEE-754 bit pattern of 1.0f.
**Pass by value copies everything**: a 4 KiB struct passed by value copies 4 KiB per call, while a pointer costs 8 bytes.
**Enum numbering**: `enum State { IDLE, RUNNING = 5, STOPPED };` gives IDLE = 0, RUNNING = 5, STOPPED = 6; unassigned names continue from the previous value plus one.

sections.heading: Variants & Types
bullets: **Plain struct**: `struct Student { ... };` used as `struct Student s;`.
**typedef struct**: `typedef struct { int a; } str1;` allows `str1 v;`; for self-reference you still need a tag: `typedef struct Node { int v; struct Node *next; } Node;`.
**Nested struct**: embed another struct as a member (`emp.addr.city`), either declared inside the parent or separately.
**Anonymous struct/union (C11)**: members promoted into the parent's namespace, so `v.i` works without an inner name.
**Flexible array member (C99)**: a last member `T data[];` sized at allocation time: `malloc(sizeof(struct Buf) + n)`.
**Bit-field**: `unsigned ready : 1;` packs flags into bits; layout is implementation-defined.
**Union**: overlaps members; used for type punning, memory saving and variants.
**Tagged union**: union plus enum discriminator, the C version of a sum type.
**Enum**: plain integer constants; use `typedef enum {...} Color;` for a type name.
**Packed struct**: `__attribute__((packed))` or `#pragma pack(1)` removes padding at the cost of slower or unaligned access; used for wire formats.

sections.heading: Complexity & Costs
bullets: **Member access**: O(1), one load at a constant offset; `p->x` is the same cost as `a[i]`.
**Copy and pass by value**: O(sizeof(struct)); copying a 64-byte struct is cheap, a 4 KiB one on every call is not.

**Size**: struct size is the sum of members plus padding, rounded up to a multiple of the largest member alignment. Example: `struct {char a; double b; char c;}` is 24 bytes; reordering to `{double b; char a; char c;}` gives 16.
**Union size**: the largest member rounded to the strictest alignment; `union {int arr[10]; char c;}` is 40 bytes, `union {int x; char y;}` is 4.
**Cache**: members accessed together should sit together (a hot/cold split into two structs can halve cache misses); arrays of structs stream well, structs of arrays suit SIMD.
**Enum cost**: zero; they compile to integer constants. The enum type's size is implementation-defined (usually 4 bytes, since constants are `int`).
**Comparison**: C has no `==` for structs; `memcmp` is O(size) but compares padding bytes, so it can give wrong answers.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls & Gotchas
bullets: **Shallow copy**: `b = a;` with a `char *name` member makes both structs point at the same string. Freeing one leaves the other dangling; write a clone function that allocates and copies.
**Forgetting `struct`**: in C, `Student s;` is an error unless you used `typedef`.
**Initializing in the definition**: `struct A { int x = 5; };` is illegal in C; initialize at the variable.
**Assigning arrays**: `s.name = "Bob";` is an error; use `strcpy`/`snprintf`, or assign the whole struct from a compound literal.
**Comparing with `memcmp` or `==`**: `==` does not compile; `memcmp` may see differing padding bytes, so compare field by field.
**`sizeof` assumptions**: do not hard-code struct sizes or offsets; use `sizeof` and `offsetof`.

**Reading the wrong union member**: after writing `i`, reading `f` reinterprets bits. It is allowed in C (not in C++) but gives a representation-dependent value, and reading a trap representation or a larger member than was written is unspecified.
**Untagged union use**: forgetting which member is active; always pair with a tag.
**Bit-field portability**: order, alignment and signedness of plain `int` fields vary, so avoid bit-fields for wire formats or hardware registers across compilers; use masks and shifts instead.

**Enum surprises**: enum constants are `int`, not scoped, and any `int` can be assigned to an enum variable without warning; two enums can silently mix. Duplicate names across enums in one scope clash.
**Passing big structs by value** to recursive functions or in hot loops; pass `const struct *`.
**Self-reference without a pointer**: `struct Node { struct Node next; };` is an infinite-size type and does not compile.

sections.heading: Real-World Use
bullets: **Data structures**: every linked list, tree, graph and hash table node is a struct with pointers (`struct Node { int val; struct Node *next; }`).
**Linux kernel**: `struct task_struct`, `struct file`, `struct list_head` embedded in other structs with `container_of`; unions in `struct page`; enums for states and error classes.
**Networking**: packet headers modeled as structs (`struct iphdr`, `struct tcphdr`) with bit-fields or explicit shifts, and unions such as `struct sockaddr_in` overlaid via `sockaddr`.
**Interpreters and parsers**: tagged unions represent AST nodes and values (`struct Value { enum Kind kind; union { long i; double d; char *s; } u; }`).
**Hardware**: unions let you view a register as a 32-bit word or as bytes; embedded code maps peripheral registers with a struct of `volatile` members.
**APIs**: `struct stat`, `struct timespec`, `struct tm`, `FILE`; opaque structs hide implementation behind a pointer and a header.

sections.heading: Interview Notes
bullets: **Struct vs union?** Struct members have separate storage and all hold values; union members share storage and only the last written is valid; union size is the largest member.
**Why can sizeof(struct) exceed the sum of members?** Alignment padding between members and at the end.
**How do you reduce struct size?** Order members from largest to smallest alignment, or pack (with a speed and portability cost).
**Dot vs arrow?** `.` on a struct value; `->` on a pointer to a struct.
**Can you assign one struct to another?** Yes, member-wise and shallow; arrays inside are copied, pointers are not deep-copied.
**What is a tagged union?** A union plus an enum that records the active member.
**Default enum values?** Start at 0 and increase by 1 unless assigned.
**Can a struct contain itself?** Only through a pointer.

subtopics.title: Defining, initializing and accessing structs
subtopics.summary: Member selection, initializer lists and designated initializers.

sections.body: Declare the type once, then create variables. An initializer list fills members in order; designated initializers (C99, not valid in older C++) name them so order does not matter, and everything left out becomes zero. You cannot give default values inside the struct definition itself.

subtopics.title: Copying structs and shallow vs deep copy

sections.body: `s2 = s1;` copies the bytes of every member, including arrays declared inline. A pointer member is copied as a pointer, so both structs now share the target. When the struct owns heap data you need a deep copy function, and a matching destroy function.

subtopics.title: Passing and returning structs
subtopics.summary: By value, by pointer, by const pointer.

sections.body: Structs are passed by value, so the callee gets its own copy and cannot change the caller's. For anything bigger than a couple of machine words, pass `const struct T *` to read and `struct T *` to modify. Returning a small struct by value is idiomatic (`struct Point make(int x, int y)`) and the compiler usually builds it directly in the caller's storage (return value optimization via a hidden pointer). Never return a pointer to a local struct.

subtopics.title: typedef, nesting and self-referential structs
subtopics.summary: Naming types and building linked structures.

sections.body: `typedef` removes the repeated `struct` keyword. A self-referential struct needs its tag inside the definition because the typedef name is not visible yet. Nested access chains dots: `p.b.c`. The nested type may be defined inside or outside the parent; defining it separately is easier to reuse.

subtopics.title: Size, padding and offsetof
subtopics.summary: Why the numbers do not add up.

sections.body: Each member must start at a multiple of its alignment, and the total size is rounded up to the largest member alignment. On common 64-bit ABIs `char` aligns to 1, `short` to 2, `int` and `float` to 4, `double`, `long` and pointers to 8. `offsetof(struct T, member)` from `<stddef.h>` reports the offset portably. Reordering members from largest to smallest usually minimizes padding. The struct-padding lesson covers packing and its trade-offs.
sections.code:
struct A { char c; int n; char d; };      // offsets 0, 4, 8 -> size 12
struct B { int n; char c; char d; };      // offsets 0, 4, 5 -> size 8
printf("%zu %zu %zu\n", sizeof(struct A), sizeof(struct B),
       offsetof(struct A, n));            // 12 8 4

sections.body: A union's members all start at offset 0. Its size is the size of the largest member (rounded for alignment). Assigning to one member makes the others hold reinterpreted bytes. In C this punning is permitted; in C++ it is undefined (use `memcpy` or `std::bit_cast`). Declaration syntax mirrors a struct, and unions can be nested or anonymous.
Using the byte view reveals endianness: on a little-endian CPU the least significant byte of the int comes first in memory.

Store an enum next to the union and always check it before reading. This is the pattern behind JSON values, interpreter objects, event structs and AST nodes. Keep creation and access in helper functions so the tag and payload cannot drift apart.

An enum numbers its constants from 0 unless you assign values; each unassigned name is the previous plus one. Constants have type `int` and share the surrounding scope, so prefix names (`COLOR_RED`) to avoid clashes. Compared with `#define` they appear in the debugger and obey scope. They are ideal for states, error codes, and flag bits.

A flexible array member (C99) is a final array with no size; allocate the header and the payload in one block so a length-prefixed buffer needs a single `malloc` and `free`. `sizeof` excludes the tail. A bit-field declares a width in bits; use it for in-memory flags, but write explicit masks for external formats because bit order and straddling rules differ across compilers.

takeaways: Struct members have separate storage and a combined size that includes alignment padding; union members overlap and the size is the largest member.
Use `.` on values and `->` on pointers; pass large structs by `const struct *` instead of copying them.
Struct assignment is a shallow copy; deep-copy any pointed-to data yourself and never compare structs with `==` or `memcmp`.
A tagged union (enum plus union) is the safe way to hold one of several types.
Enum constants are `int` values starting at 0 and are unscoped; use prefixes and explicit values for flags.
Order members from largest to smallest alignment to cut padding, and use `offsetof` instead of hard-coded offsets.
Bit-fields and packed structs are implementation-specific, so avoid them for portable wire or register formats.
